opening.headline: Instead of rewriting from scratch when you don't like the first result, learn how to make only the necessary changes with specific feedback.
body: If you don't like the first results from AI, many people delete the request and rewrite it from scratch. However, the result of the newly written request is that the tone improves, but the good structure disappears, and the tone may change again next time.

In this lesson, we'll look at the difference between feedback that's vague, like "better," and feedback that's specific, like "spend the second paragraph in two sentences." Next, we determine how to identify and correct problems in the results among instructions, context, and format, criteria for deciding whether to correct or rewrite, and success criteria to determine whether the improved results are sufficient.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the flow of iterative improvement (from feedback to correction)
You can distinguish whether to fix a problem in the results: instructions, context, or format.
You can determine whether the improved results are sufficient

screens.title: If you don't like it, rewrite it from the beginning.
screens.lead: Move the sliders and see how the results change each time you write from scratch.

visual.alt: A scene where the request is erased and rewritten below the first result card, followed by the second and third result cards.
labels: Delete the entire request and rewrite it

data.controlLabel: Number of times rewritten from scratch

stops.body: The first result was that the composition was well structured, but the tone was overly rigid. Users didn't like this one thing. The only thing that needs to be fixed is the tone, and the user decides to throw away the entire result.

The user erased the entire request and rewrote it from scratch with a request to soften the tone. The second result has a better tone, but the structure that was good in the first result is gone. The only thing that was asked to be changed was the tone, but even the composition was changed.

The composition was disappointing, so I requested it again from the beginning. This time, some of the composition is back, but the tone is different again. Even with the same request, the results are slightly different each time, so if you rewrite the whole thing, even the good parts are shaken.

Should I tell them where to fix it so that only the parts that need to be changed? What is needed now is not to rewrite the request from scratch, but to point out the problematic parts and fix them. In this class you will learn how.

screens.outro: First, let's think about how you have asked for corrections so far.

screens.title: How did you ask to correct the disappointing results?
screens.lead: Read the questions below and answer them in your head. There are no fields to enter or submit.

paragraphs: How did you request corrections when the results were disappointing? Have you ever used words like “write better” or “do it again”?
Or did you point out which part is the problem? For example, “the second paragraph is too long,” which is a way of saying both the location and the reason.

Think about how the results you received from the two methods were different. Think as much as you remember whether only the place you asked for was changed or whether other places were also changed. On this screen, you don't have to write down your answer, just think about it. It is not a time to find the right answer, but a time to reflect on your habits.

callout.label: Organizing the instructor's thoughts
callout.text: Even when giving feedback to people, “Move the conclusion to the front” is much more useful than “Try to do better.” The same goes for models. Feedback should include what to change and how to change it.

screens.outro: Let’s compare directly to see what difference specific feedback makes.

screens.title: “Better” and “Second paragraph in two sentences.”
screens.lead: Tap the switch to compare the modifications made with vague and specific feedback.

states.label: vague feedback
states.body:
Edit Request: “Write it better.”

The model doesn't know what the problem is, so it guesses what to change. You can make your sentences more elaborate, increase their length, or change their structure entirely. As a result, even the good parts may be shaken, and the changes desired by users may not occur.

The Gemini Guide explains that even if you change the expression in a sentence with the same meaning, the response will change, and it introduces an iterative strategy of changing the wording when the result is different from expectations. However, vague words without a definite direction to change are the least effective of all attempts.

states.label: specific feedback
states.body:
Edit request: “Please shorten the second paragraph to two sentences. Leave the rest as is.”

It's clear where to change (second paragraph), what to do (two sentences), and what not to touch (the rest). As a result, only the requested parts are changed and the good parts remain the same. This is the same principle that Claude guides say when explaining the desired output more specifically, the better the result.

Feedback should include three things: what, where, and how. If you have these three things, your model doesn't have to guess. This is the key to specificity. Conversely, if even one is missing, the blank space is filled with guesses.

screens.outro: Let's look at the overall flow of repeating feedback and the success criteria that determine where to stop.

screens.title: Flow and success criteria of iterative improvement
screens.lead: By selecting the numbered markers in the picture, you can see what is done at each step of the iterative improvement. Please select them in order starting from number 1.

visual.alt: A schematic with a cycle of results, diagnosis, feedback, and correction, with success criteria placed in the center.
labels: Example: one sentence, 40 characters or less, polite expression

markers.label: result
markers.title: Read the results you received
markers.body: Read the results against your success criteria before requesting modifications. Don't just look at what you like, but mark what you like and what you don't like. The good parts become the parts that need to be kept.

markers.label: diagnosis
markers.title: Locate the problem
markers.body: I'm not sure if the disappointing part is because of the instructions, context, or format. How to fix it varies depending on the cause. Skipping this diagnosis leads to vague feedback like “better.”

markers.label: feedback
markers.title: Give specific feedback
markers.body: Write down where and how to change. It also tells you what parts you should not change. The Gemini Guide introduces repetition strategies such as changing expressions, replacing with similar tasks, and changing the order of content, and asks you to compare the different results after making changes.

markers.label: revision
markers.title: I will receive a revised copy and check again.
markers.body: When a revised version arrives, we check it again using the same criteria. You can tell if things have improved by looking at them by the same standards. The OpenAI guide instructs you to manage prompts like code and check them before and after changes, and the same attitude is needed for iterative improvements made by humans.

markers.label: success criteria
markers.title: Decide where to stop
markers.body: Success criteria are the conditions under which we determine whether the results are sufficient. For example, if you say something like "one sentence, 40 characters or less, polite" in advance, you can decide where to stop the repetition. Without standards, improvements continue endlessly, and it is difficult to determine which revision is better.

screens.outro: Let's take a look at the table to see how to identify the problem spot and decide whether to fix it or rewrite it.

screens.title: Identify the problem and decide how to fix it
screens.lead: The table below divides the resulting problems into instructions, context, and format, and summarizes the criteria for deciding whether to correct or rewrite them. Read along the lines and connect the symptoms with the fix.

data.caption: How to diagnose and fix problems in the results
rows: instructions
I was vague about what to do, so I did the wrong thing.
Re-write specifically what needs to be done and the standards.
“Make a comparison table, not a summary.”
context
There was no background or data, so I came up with a general theory.
Additional background and materials are provided.
“Our customer is an office worker in his 20s. Please refer to this information.”
format
The content is correct, but the framework and length are different.
Specify format and quantity.
“Please shorten the second paragraph to two sentences.”
Next, when choosing to fix
The overall direction is correct, but only some parts are disappointing.
Leave the good parts alone and only point out the problem parts.
“The composition is the same, only the tone is respectful.”
When to choose to rewrite
The direction was wrong from the beginning.
Rewrite your request, incorporating what you learned from previous results.
“Write from the beginning, changing readers from executives to customers.”
data.notes: ChatGPT personalized guidelines apply the same request to all conversations, and changes are reflected in future conversations. If you are repeatedly giving the same feedback, you can also write it down in custom instructions. It is appropriate to continue making corrections within a single conversation, and to rewrite when the direction itself is wrong.

screens.outro: Let’s apply what we’ve learned to the example of improving your marketing copy three times.

screens.title: Commentary: The first improvement in marketing copy
screens.lead: An instructor walks you through the process of improving your lunch reservation service's marketing copy, step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed.

steps.title: draft
steps.body: The first result was “Best quality, best service! Try it now.” The format is correct for a one-line advertisement, but there is no clue as to what is good for whom. This is a phrase that can be attached to any service.

steps.title: diagnosis
steps.body: The place of concern is instruction. The request was vague enough to “write me some marketing copy,” so the model filled in the most generic promotional copy. What is missing is the object and its merits, not its composition or form.

steps.title: Feedback and Success Criteria
steps.body: The feedback is, “To customers who are office workers in their 20s, please describe the advantage of saving 10 minutes during lunch in one sentence.” The success criterion is set as one sentence, 40 characters or less. The target, benefits, and quantity are all included.

steps.title: Revisions and Instructor’s Judgment
steps.body: The revised copy is "Skip lunch lines and save 10 minutes." (37 characters, including spaces and punctuation). It states the benefit and meets the one-sentence, 40-character limit. The instructor chooses to keep revising because the structure works; only the wording needs refinement. Starting over could lose that useful structure. The success criteria provide a consistent way to judge each revision.

screens.outro: Next, we will look at the second and third improvements and sufficiency judgments.

screens.title: Commentary: Second and third improvements and sufficiency judgment
screens.lead: When you select each item, the request statement, modification results, and whether or not the success criteria are met are displayed. Judge for yourself and then click to compare.

items.prompt: Second improvement: What did you ask for after diagnosing that your tone was stiff?
items.answer: The feedback is: "Make it warmer and polite, as if speaking to a friend. Keep the audience and benefit." The revision is "You get ten more minutes for lunch. Please pick up your pre-ordered lunch without waiting in line!" (98 characters). The tone improves, but the copy now has two sentences and exceeds 40 characters. Changing the tone caused the writer to lose track of the sentence and length constraints.

items.prompt: Third improvement: What did you do when the length exceeded the standard?
items.answer: Next, the request is: "Keep the time-saving benefit and polite tone, but reduce it to one sentence of at most 35 characters." The revision is "Please skip lines and save 10 min." (34 characters). It preserves the benefit while meeting both the sentence and length constraints.

items.prompt: How do I check if this result is sufficient?
items.answer: Check the success criteria you initially set one by one. Is it one sentence, is it 40 characters or less, does it contain some positive points toward office workers in their 20s, or is it a friendly polite way of speaking? This revision satisfies all four requirements.

items.prompt: What if I meet the criteria and still want to fix it?
items.answer: First, check to see if there was anything new that bothered you in the criteria. If your taste is not in the standards, add it as a new standard and judge again. For example, if “I want the number to come first” is important, add it to the criteria and edit it one more time. If it's not important enough to include in the criteria, it's okay to stop here.
Setting standards helps you determine when to end, and specific feedback creates specific improvements. Notice that all three improvements were subsequent fixes rather than rewrites.

screens.outro: Lastly, I will summarize the contents of this class.

screens.title: Criteria for improving results with feedback
screens.lead: We organize the contents so far into inspection criteria for iterative improvement.

paragraphs: Concrete feedback creates concrete improvements. Feedback should include where and how to change and what not to change. The reason why the initial “rewrite from scratch” was always wrong was because everything was handed over again without specifying where to fix it.

Before modifying, try to identify the problem location first. If what needs to be done is ambiguous, I change the instructions, if there is a general theory, I change the context, and if the content is correct but the framework is different, I change the format. If the overall direction is correct, continue to correct it, and rewrite only if the direction is wrong from the beginning.

Lastly, set your success criteria in advance. One sentence, 40 characters or less, and verifiable conditions such as an honorific expression are sufficient. Having a baseline allows you to judge for yourself whether your revisions have improved and whether you can stop now. Iterative improvement is ultimately about repeating four things. We read the results against the standards, diagnose the problem, provide specific feedback, and check the revised version again against the same standards. Getting this cycle in place will greatly reduce the need to rewrite requests from scratch. If you have feedback that you repeat often, it's a good idea to write it down in custom or project instructions so you don't say the same thing every time.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Identify the problem location, fix it, and determine whether it is sufficient as a success criterion.

glossary.def: The process of seeing the results, providing feedback, and receiving revisions is repeated.
It's just a matter of pointing out the location and standards to fix.
These are checkable conditions set in advance to determine whether the results are sufficient.
This is a method of requesting corrections only to problematic parts of the existing results.

misconceptions.myth: If you don't like it, the fastest way is to rewrite it from scratch.
misconceptions.fact: You may lose the good parts or shake up other parts. If the overall direction is correct, it is more efficient to point out only the problematic parts and then fix them.

misconceptions.myth: If you say, “Make it better,” it will get better on its own.
misconceptions.fact: Without a baseline, the model guesses what to change. Only by writing down where and how to change can you achieve the desired improvement.

misconceptions.myth: There is no end to improvement.
misconceptions.fact: If you set your success criteria in advance, you can stop when you meet them. Tastes that are not included in the standards are added as new standards and re-evaluated.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Determine whether the problem with the result lies in instructions, context, or format and correct it.
If the overall direction is correct, continue to correct it, and rewrite only if the direction is wrong.
Establishing success criteria allows you to determine whether the results are sufficient and whether you can stop.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What is the feedback I've been given so far telling me to fix?

checks.q: If the result is 'the content is correct, but the table frame and amount are different', what is the problem?
checks.explain: If the content is correct but the frame or length is different, it is a format issue. If the instructions are vague, you'll end up with random things, and if there's no context, you'll end up with generalities.

wrong.0: An instruction problem is when the wrong thing to do is done because the task to be done is ambiguous.
wrong.1: A context problem is when a general theory is made without background or data.
wrong.3: The content itself is correct, so it is not a question of up-to-dateness.

checks.intro: Think about the problem and choose the appropriate option. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: 'Best quality, best service!' I'm trying to edit the draft. What is the most effective feedback?
options: ‘In one sentence, tell customers who are office workers in their 20s the benefit of saving 10 minutes during lunch time.’
‘If you don’t like it, please rewrite it from the beginning.’
checks.explain: Feedback should include what and how to change. If you specify the target, benefits, and quantity, you can leave a good composition and only change the necessary parts.

wrong.0: It's vague, leaving you to guess what the model will change.
wrong.2: When the composition is good, I continue to revise it rather than rewrite it.

checks.intro: Think about the specific conditions for feedback and choose an appropriate option. Results are not recorded.
checks.incorrectFeedback: It's unfortunate, but other options are better.
